source: Andrews & Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models
finding: Label-free Dutch-book test: an arbitrageur LP finds the guaranteed profit against a model's stated probabilities. Models are often incoherent on stock-return bin events.
numbers: Baseline GPT-OSS-120B, 100 stock-days, 14 questions: mean profit 0.002067 per unit stake (95% CI 0.001471-0.002737). Profit >=0.1% in 48/100, >=0.5% in 15, >=1% in 6. 15 models, 365,100 elicitations. Rounding to 4 decimals can give at most 5e-5.
limits: One domain (stock returns), mostly one model for the prompt experiments. Profit is an incoherence measure, not tradable money.
agent_relevance: Coherence can be checked in code with no answer key. A cheap check for any set of related probabilities the agent emits.

source: Andrews & Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models
finding: Incoherence varies much more across models than accuracy does, but the two rank together.
numbers: Profit ranges about 100x, from 0.002067 (GPT-OSS-120B) to 0.1994 (Mistral Small 3.2). Brier only 0.1966 to 0.2157. Spearman 0.9143. 101 of 105 pairwise profit gaps exclude zero versus 32 for Brier.
limits: One pass per non-workhorse model. Lookahead bias in newer models may touch Brier but not profit. Ordering may change with elicitation.
agent_relevance: Coherence discriminates models better than Brier, so it can be a cheap probe for which model to use in a probability slot.

source: Andrews & Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models
finding: Richer logical links between events raise incoherence. Adding joint-event questions across two stocks raised profit significantly.
numbers: 50 dates; joint cells added to two-stock marginals raised mean profit by 0.00244 (CI 0.001971-0.002961). Horizon preamble also changed coherence of the same question.
limits: Effect shown for GPT-OSS-120B; matched-query check in Appendix D.
agent_relevance: The more the schema asks about overlapping events in one call, the more checks it needs. Keep hypothesis sets small and exclusive.

source: Andrews & Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models
finding: Asking about all 14 events in one query drives incoherence nearly to zero. Asking complement pairs together also lowers it. Relation-poor pairs raise it.
numbers: Full-panel arm: remaining incoherence about rounding level. Complement-pair arm: significant decrease. Relation-poor pair arm: significant increase.
limits: Single model and one question panel. Users rarely query this way.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G5: elicit the whole exclusive answer set in one call and normalise in code. Do not ask for each option in a separate call.

source: Andrews & Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models
finding: Irrelevant context raises incoherence. Notes like an intuitive 70% anchor, positive emotion, anxiety, phone battery 70%, or coffee all increased profit. Averaging five passes helped only a little because 95% of answers were identical across passes.
numbers: Seven irrelevant-context arms; most significant increases, abstract says up to an order of magnitude. Largest: gut-feeling 70% anchor and positive emotion. Averaging K=1..5 gave modest gains.
limits: Magnitude per arm read from figure, not a table. Some arms (emotion about a stock) may carry weak information.
agent_relevance: Keep the probability slot free of user chatter, anchors and persona text. Resampling does not fix incoherence; structure does.

source: Andrews & Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models
finding: Information in the prompt can hurt coherence. A procedure instruction and a news headline raised profit a lot; adding bin statistics lowered it.
numbers: Statistics arm: significant decrease. Instructions arm: large significant increase. Identity: small increase. Headline: large increase.
limits: Single model, one task.
agent_relevance: Adding more text is not free. Test each added prompt element for coherence cost at equal tokens (G7).

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Arbitrage-based consistency metric on logically linked forecasts (Negation, Paraphrase, Consequence, AndOr, And, Or, Cond, CondCond). Consistency correlates with later Brier score.
numbers: Aggregate correlation in figure 0.92 for one metric; Cond check R above 0.9 (0.92 in table), other checks little signal. Forecasters with Brier worse than 0.25 excluded from the correlation.
limits: Excluding the worst forecasters favours the correlation. Few forecasters. The long-term benchmark resolves in 2028.
agent_relevance: Consistency can proxy accuracy when no answer key exists. Conditional-probability checks are the most informative.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: ArbitrageForecaster: patch a base forecaster by arbitraging its outputs on a check (recursively). It fixes the check it targets but does not generalise.
numbers: gpt-4o-mini base, recursion depth r=0..4. Gain largest for Negation, then Paraphrase, lowest for ExpEvidence. No reliable improvement in ground-truth Brier or on checks not targeted.
limits: Few setups tested because of cost. Authors note forecasting 50% everywhere passes some checks.
agent_relevance: Coherence repair alone is not accuracy. Goodhart risk: a fixer can pass checks and stay wrong. Pair with G3 held-out checks.

source: Fluri, Paleka, Tramer (2023) Evaluating Superhuman Models with Consistency Checks
finding: GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 violate negation, paraphrase, monotonicity and Bayes-rule consistency in forecasting at temperature 0.
numbers: Strong violation (>0.2) rate, GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4: Negation 52.6% vs 10.9% (mean 0.34 vs 0.10); Paraphrase 30.8% vs 12.5%; Monotonicity 42.0% vs 16.0%; Bayes rule 68.6% vs 58.8% (means 0.28 vs 0.25).
limits: Randomness explains under 20% of strong violations. Early models (2023).
agent_relevance: Bigger models fix simple checks (negation) far more than the Bayes-rule check. Complement coherence does not guarantee conditional coherence.

source: Fluri, Paleka, Tramer (2023) Evaluating Superhuman Models with Consistency Checks
finding: Prompting the model to be consistent on one check fixes that check and can hurt another.
numbers: GPT-4 negation prompting: negation violations 10.9% to 2.9% (mean 0.10 to 0.06), but paraphrase 12.5% to 17.3% and Bayes rule 58.8% to 68.6%. GPT-3.5 paraphrase prompting: paraphrase 30.8% to 37.5% (worse), Bayes 68.6% to 45.1%.
limits: Single temperature, two models.
agent_relevance: A prompt that says 'make probabilities sum to 1' may trade off other coherence. Enforce sums in code, not by prompt.

source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024) Incoherent Probability Judgments in Large Language Models
finding: Four LLMs show human-like incoherence on probabilistic identities (Z1..Z8) built from P(A), P(B), P(A and B), P(A or B). Deviation grows with the imbalance of positive and negative terms. Mean-variance of repeated judgments is an inverted U, like humans.
numbers: 24 event pairs (12 weather, 12 politics), GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo-1106, LLaMA-2 7B and 70B, temperature 0 and 1, five repeats. Larger models deviate less but none reach zero. Bayesian Sampler fits better than PT+N.
limits: Numbers are in figures only. Judgments were single-number replies with no reasoning.
agent_relevance: Explains why separate single-event probabilities drift: a shrinkage prior toward 0.5. Another reason to normalise in code.

source: Freedman & Toni (2025) Exploring the Potential for LLMs to Demonstrate Rational Probabilistic Beliefs
finding: Models fail complementarity (P(A)+P(not A)=1) and monotonicity on a new claims dataset. Direct prompting, chain-of-thought, argumentative LLMs and top-5 logit sampling all tested.
numbers: Complementarity, share of predictions off by >5% / >10% / >15%, averages over models: direct 0.856/0.721/0.640; CoT 0.863/0.727/0.646; ArgLLM 0.833/0.711/0.599. Llama-3 direct 0.965/0.942/0.905. GPT-4o-mini logit sampling 0.729/0.549/0.441. 400 claim pairs per task, 1200 samples.
limits: Claims with indeterminate truth. Authors say scaling alone will not remove the failure.
agent_relevance: Chain-of-thought did not fix complement coherence. Forced normalisation in code does what reasoning text did not.

source: Imran et al. (2025) Are LLM Belief Updates Consistent with Bayes' Theorem?
finding: Bayesian Coherence Coefficient (BCC, correlation of observed vs expected in-context update) rises with scale across five pre-trained model families.
numbers: BCC vs log parameters r=0.906, p<1e-6. 6,460 instances. Llama 3 1.24B 0.658, 8.03B 0.739; Qwen2.5 3.09B 0.667, 14.77B 0.743; Falcon3 1.67B 0.594, 10.31B 0.688; GPT-2 0.14B 0.477, 1.61B 0.595. BCC vs training steps not significant.
limits: Base (pre-trained only) models up to 14B, not instruction-tuned. Direction agreement only 64-76%.
agent_relevance: Small models update in the right direction but weakly. Do not trust small-model probability updates without code.

source: Filbry, Melo, Gal (2026) From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
finding: Coherence depends on whether elicitation is across conversations or inside one dialogue. Across separate conversations, Dutch-bookable violations (normalisation, monotonicity, extensionality) exceed 50% of 30 scenarios for almost all model-axiom pairs. Inside one dialogue they drop to 10% for Gemini and one scenario of 30 for Gemma.
numbers: 30 scenarios, three modern LLMs, three axioms N, M, E.
limits: Small scenario set; authors do not claim universal coherence. Result 1: reasoning LLMs generally satisfy the axioms within a dialogue.
agent_relevance: Keep all related probabilities in ONE context so the model sees its earlier numbers. Separate samples or separate agents lose coherence (fits G4).

source: Filbry, Melo, Gal (2026) From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
finding: Without reasoning, in-context Bayesian updates drift from the true posterior and cut task success. Native reasoning closes most of the gap; code execution handles intractable posteriors.
numbers: Non-reasoning LLM updates reduced final success by at least 30% across settings (20Q and ProteinWorld). With reasoning: near-exact closed-form posteriors and consistency over ten evidence items. Gemini-2.5-Pro with code approximates ProteinWorld-hard posteriors well.
limits: Synthetic environments. Authors argue strict harnesses (BED-LLM) may be unnecessary for reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Partly against rigid code scaffolds for belief updating. Use code for arithmetic (G5) but let a reasoning model set up the update.

source: Dragonevskiy (2026) Understanding as No-Arbitrage: Bounded Dutch Books as a Definition and Training Objective
finding: Pre-registered tests on small instruction-tuned models. Within-format credences are close to coherent; cross-format and negation books extract guaranteed profit.
numbers: Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B and SmolLM3-3B, 9,360 elicitations each. Pre-registered median Inc 0.024 (1.5B, CI 0.019-0.032), 0.000 (3B), 0.0001 (7B), 0.019 (SmolLM3): kill threshold 0.05 fired. Cross-format book mean profit 0.151, 0.021, 0.064, 0.070. 25.0% of propositions at 1.5B had profit above 0.25.
limits: Single-author preprint. Authors admit near-zero incoherence at 7B coincides with near-maximal confidence (confident degeneration).
agent_relevance: Low incoherence can be fake: a degenerate confident model is coherent for free. Check coherence together with calibration or accuracy.

source: Dragonevskiy (2026) Understanding as No-Arbitrage: Bounded Dutch Books as a Definition and Training Objective
finding: Training against an exact Dutch-book adversary (Arbitr) cuts negation exploitability by two orders of magnitude, but half the runs collapsed until a calibration term was added.
numbers: E-A1: negation exploitability down about 100x; half the runs collapse to an uninformative equilibrium. E-A1b adds a calibration term: all registered criteria pass with no task accuracy cost. Anchor alone explains a factor of about 2.4 on negation; replicates on Phi-3.5.
limits: Small models (1.5B-7B), preprint, wording-specific residue. Hallucination untouched.
agent_relevance: If coherence is ever trained, add a calibration term. Not usable by a scaffold-only agent, but shows the failure mode to guard.

source: Andrews (2026) Revealed Rationality: Label-Free Evaluation and Regularization from Representation Theorems
finding: Argues de Finetti's theorem gives a complete, label-free coherence penalty for evaluation and training; also covers Afriat (preferences) and Echenique-Saito (SEU). Cites related LLM work.
numbers: Cites Tak et al. (2026): LLMs violate vNM axioms widely, but more reasoning tokens substantially improve axiom compliance. Cites Chadwick et al. (2025): incoherent probabilities and intransitive preferences in LLMs.
limits: Position paper. Coherence does not pick which objective rationalises behaviour, so it complements accuracy signals.
agent_relevance: Passing a de Finetti check exhausts what coherence can say. It cannot show the numbers are right.

source: Williamson, Foti et al. (2026) LLMs are not (consistently) Bayesian: quantifying internal (in)consistencies
finding: Measures an information-processing gap between an LLM's post-evidence beliefs and what it thinks the evidence contains. Some update methods are near-Bayesian; others are learned heuristics that often beat exact Bayesian updates on downstream tasks.
numbers: Abstract and intro read; figures show batch updating usually outperforms belief propagation. 95% bootstrap error bars. Per-model near-perfect vs unreliable percentages are in figures, not extracted.
limits: Not all numbers extracted; models include GPT-5.1 variants.
agent_relevance: Exact Bayesian arithmetic over model-supplied likelihoods can be worse than the model's implicit update. Misspecified likelihoods are the weak point.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models (Nature Communications)
finding: Fine-tuning LLMs to mimic a Bayesian assistant makes them update beliefs far better and transfers to new tasks. Off-the-shelf LLMs show limited or no improvement across rounds of a flight-recommendation task.
numbers: Bayesian-tuned LLMs agree with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time, more than original or oracle-tuned models. Models: Gemma 2 9B/27B, Llama 3 8B/70B, Qwen 2.5 7B/32B; human participants improve from round 1 to 5 (p=0.002).
limits: Needs training; not a scaffold method. Task is preference inference.
agent_relevance: Shows the gap is learnable, but our agent cannot train. Argues for code-side update steps.

source: Betz & Richardson (2023) Probabilistic coherence, logical consistency, and Bayesian learning: Neural language models as epistemic agents (PLOS ONE 18(2):e0281372)
finding: Abstract level only (full text blocked this session): T5 rankers trained on synthetic corpora; self-training on auto-generated texts gradually yields probabilistically coherent belief systems and helps evidential learning.
numbers: No numbers extracted. Search snippet states current pre-trained NLMs are not doxastic agents.
limits: Synthetic corpora, T5 rankers, not general chat LLMs.
agent_relevance: Precedent for coherence training. Read full text before citing numbers.

source: Mandel, Karvetski, Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy (JDM 13(6)), as logged in our earlier claims file
finding: Human analysts: forcing probabilities over exclusive hypotheses to sum to 1 cut error about 35%; averaging analysts after that cut error about 61%.
numbers: 50 analysts. Source of the G5 figure. Earlier note: plain normalisation (0.13) did as well as coherentization.
limits: Not reopened this session. Human data, one task; the 35% has no LLM measurement yet.
agent_relevance: G5 rests on human data. The LLM papers here support it indirectly (coherence correlates with accuracy), but no one has measured the 35% on LLM answer sets.

source: Li & Sreedhar (2026) Outcome-free arbitrage audits and coherence repairs for LLM forecasters (ICML 2026 workshop)
finding: Cited by Filbry et al. as an arbitrage-audit and repair method for LLM forecasters. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Title and citation only.
agent_relevance: Another candidate for a coherence-repair step; read before use.

source: Matta, Naphade, Zou (2026) Rethinking LLM confidence: From calibration to coherence (ICML 2026 workshop)
finding: Cited by Filbry et al. as arguing for coherence over calibration for confidence. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Citation only.
agent_relevance: Possible support for judging confidence by coherence.

source: Tak et al. (2026) vNM axiom tests of LLMs, as described in Andrews (2026)
finding: Second-hand: LLMs widely violate vNM axioms (completeness, transitivity, continuity, independence); more reasoning tokens substantially improve compliance.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Second-hand via Andrews; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Hints that extra thinking helps preference coherence, but G11 warns it can hurt elsewhere.

source: Chadwick, Kahng, Kipper (2025) Dutch books and money pumps: Rectifying vulnerabilities in LLMs through rationality (HAR 2025)
finding: Second-hand via Andrews and Sarkar: observes incoherent probability assessments and intransitive preferences in LLMs. The paper itself was not found by search.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not located; do not cite beyond this.
agent_relevance: Money-pump framing for LLM agents; unverified.
